summary: Defines a SASL authentication mechanism based on ISO/IEC 9798-3 and FIPS PUB 196 entity authentication. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: It adds another way to prove who you are when you log in.

subtitle: A SASL authentication mechanism based on public key signatures using X.509 certificates.

tldr.problem: Most authentication protocols like CRAM-MD5 require shared secrets maintained at both server and client, but using public keys could allow a client to prove identity with only a private key.
tldr.mechanism: This SASL mechanism uses X.509 certificates and digital signatures following ISO/IEC 9798-3 standards. In unilateral mode, the client signs a server challenge; in mutual mode, both parties exchange signed challenges to prove their identity to each other.
tldr.outcome: While the mechanism was documented and registered, the IESG noted it provided authentication without the integrity protection of TLS, creating a less secure alternative with the complexity of public key infrastructure.

today: RFC 3163 is experimental. The IESG discouraged using this mechanism in Internet protocols, recommending TLS/SSL instead, which provides authentication with integrity and confidentiality. The mechanism has seen minimal deployment; TLS and other standards-track authentication protocols are preferred. The underlying ISO/IEC 9798-3 standard remains valid for other applications, but this SASL binding has not become widely used.

sections.title: Public Key Authentication via SASL
sections.content:
RFC 3163 defines a SASL (Simple Authentication and Security Layer) mechanism that uses asymmetric (public key) cryptography for authentication. SASL is a framework for adding authentication to protocols like IMAP, SMTP, and LDAP. Unlike password-based SASL mechanisms that require both client and server to know a shared secret, this mechanism only requires the client to have a private key and the server to trust the client's X.509 certificate.

The mechanism provides authentication only; it does not encrypt traffic or protect message integrity. The IESG noted in the RFC that this is a mismatch: it has all the deployment complexity of public key infrastructure (PKI) but loses the security benefits of TLS (which provides authentication, integrity, and confidentiality). The intended use is where encryption is provided by lower-layer protocols or the application itself.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a way to sign in using your private key. Instead of sending a password, you sign a challenge from the server, and it verifies your signature to know it is really you.

sections.title: Two Modes: Unilateral and Mutual
sections.content:
The mechanism defines two authentication modes. In unilateral mode, the server sends a random challenge to the client. The client generates its own random number, creates an X.509 certificate (or uses an existing one), and signs both its random number and the server's challenge with its private key. The client sends this signed token to the server. The server verifies the signature, checks that the server's challenge appears in the signed data, and optionally verifies that the server identity matches its own.

In mutual mode, the client and server authenticate each other. After the unilateral exchange, the server creates a token containing a third random number, its certificate, and a signature over the client's and server's random numbers plus the new number. This allows the client to verify the server in the same way.
sections.plainLanguage: Unilateral: you sign a message to prove you are you. Mutual: both you and the server sign messages so each can be sure of the other.

sections.title: The Protocol Messages
sections.content:
The mechanism uses three main message types. The server initiates by sending TokenBA1, which contains a random challenge and optionally the server's identity and preferred certificate authorities. The client responds with TokenAB, containing a random value, its X.509 certificate (or chain), an optional authorization identity (if different from the certificate subject), and a digital signature over the challenge and client's random value.

In mutual mode, the server sends TokenBA2 containing a new random value, the server's certificate, and a signature. All messages are DER-encoded (a binary encoding standard for ASN.1 structures). The mechanism supports three signature algorithms: RSA-SHA1-ENC, DSA-SHA1, and ECDSA-SHA1, with RSA recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a challenge, the client signs it with its private key and sends its certificate, and the server checks the signature. In mutual mode, the server also signs something so the client can check the server.

sections.title: Security Limitations and Concerns
sections.content:
The mechanism protects only against passive eavesdropping: an attacker who records the exchange cannot forge new authentication without the client's private key. However, it provides no defense against active attacks. A man-in-the-middle can intercept and modify messages, and the mechanism offers no integrity protection for data after authentication.

The IESG noted in the document that the mechanism has significant drawbacks. It requires a full PKI deployment (issuing, validating, and trusting X.509 certificates) but provides no integrity or confidentiality, whereas TLS provides all three. The use of random numbers (R_A, R_B, R_C) is critical: if random numbers are predictable, an attacker can forge signatures or replay attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone is listening to your network, they cannot trick you because they cannot sign messages. But if they are actively changing messages, this mechanism does not stop them. Also, you have to set up a whole certificate system just to get basic authentication.

sections.title: SASL Mechanism Registration
sections.content:
The RFC registers six SASL mechanism names with IANA: 9798-U-RSA-SHA1-ENC, 9798-M-RSA-SHA1-ENC, 9798-U-DSA-SHA1, 9798-M-DSA-SHA1, 9798-U-ECDSA-SHA1, and 9798-M-ECDSA-SHA1. The U indicates unilateral authentication and M indicates mutual authentication. Each mechanism can be used with the designated algorithm.

An example shows the mechanism in use with IMAP4. The client sends an AUTHENTICATE command with the mechanism name, the server responds with a base64-encoded challenge, and the client sends a base64-encoded token response. Upon successful verification, the server responds with OK and logs in the authenticated user.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism is officially registered as a SASL option that IMAP, SMTP, and other protocols can use. It has six registered variants for different signature algorithms.
